title: Karolína Muchová edges past Coco Gauff in stunning tiebreak to reach first Wimbledon final
content:
THE ALL ENGLAND CLUB, London — Coco Gauff is a two-time Grand Slam champion who leads the WTA in three-set wins this year. She had beaten Karolína Muchová six of the seven times they had played.

But it was Muchová who won their eighth meeting on the biggest stage yet — Centre Court at Wimbledon — to reach her first final. Muchová will be back there Saturday to play either Ukraine’s Marta Kostyuk or her Czech compatriot, Linda Nosková, after she defeated Gauff 6-2, 1-6, 7-6(12-10) by edging through a nail-biting deciding set and tiebreak.

Muchová took a 3-1 lead on a crouching forehand volley that just plopped into court — and even she shook her head after that. She’d dive for a volley again for a 5-3 lead, but Gauff would not quit, and they traded points back and forth for a long while. Both were tight: Muchová received a time violation while serving at 8-8, and Gauff had match point at 9-8 but flubbed a forehand pat into the net.

Muchová had match point at 10-9 and came into the net, where Gauff came up with an improbable passing shot that Muchová decided to leave — and it found the back corner.

But finally, at 11-10, Gauff could do no more. Muchová found the will to dictate one last rally, just as she had dictated her first match point. She sent Gauff scurrying around the court, chasing down the ball. Again, Gauff had to hit a forehand on the run. Again, Muchová came forward to the net.

This time, the ball thudded into the net and Muchová fell to the floor with the joy of it.

For the American, the loss carries an undeniable silver lining. The 22-year-old was long considered ill-suited for grass, given how the surface dulls the athletic foundation of her game and rushes her forehand.

“Regardless of how the rest of this tournament goes, I really think I’ve found a bit of a breakthrough on grass,” Gauff said earlier this week, while clarifying she still wanted to win the title.

She didn’t, but she made considerable progress.

Muchová, the 29-year-old No. 10 seed, appears to be a natural grass-court player, given her versatility, slice, prowess at net and mid-point creativity. Watching Muchová when she’s in the zone is sublime, but counter to her innate abilities, she hasn’t often gotten the chance to show her best work on grass.

She shared the same frustrating history at Wimbledon as her opponent Thursday, who is considered the opposite of a grass-court savant.

Before this year, Gauff had never made it past the fourth round, a loaded milestone because it is the stage she reached at her first Wimbledon in 2019. She fell in the first round in 2023 and 2025.

Before 2026, Muchová hadn’t logged a single win at Wimbledon since her run to the quarterfinal in 2021. But both players zipped and fought their way through the draw to the semifinals, having taken opposite routes to the tournament. Muchová won the grass-court Bad Homburg Tennis Open in Germany; Gauff lost the opening match of her tuneup event and then chose to practice instead of competing.

Their obstacles during the past fortnight have been somewhat similar. Muchová eased through three matches before she ran into her countrywoman Barbora Krejčíková, the 2024 Wimbledon champion, in a fourth-round meeting that exposed a vulnerability: Muchová’s occasional struggles to close out matches.

Twice, she was two points away from winning the match, first on Krejčíková’s serve, then on her own, where instead she hit a double fault. She needed three sets to seal the win.

Lately, Gauff can relate. She spoke at the French Open about recent struggles with not being aggressive enough in crucial, close-out moments in matches.

At Wimbledon, although she often had to grind through three sets to win, she has focused on being aggressive, even if it does not always work out — especially on her serve, which is one of the deadliest in the game but can also produce double faults.

Entering Thursday’s match, Gauff led the field with 29 double faults, 21 more than her semifinal opponent. But she was also hitting her first serve at an average of roughly 113 mph, the fastest of any woman in the draw.

Equally important as the tactical advantage of a big serve is what it unlocks for the rest of her game. Going for her serve puts Gauff in an aggressive mindset, and the brain space she would normally reserve for fretting about getting her first serve in and not double-faulting is free to be used elsewhere.

“I think it’s much easier to start the points off when you’re on the offensive than if you just get it in and you’re hoping the girl misses,” Gauff said in a news conference after her third-round win.

“At this level, it’s not going to happen, especially now in the second week.”

The only problem for Gauff in Thursday’s semifinal was that her power was going against placement and accuracy. Muchová had served the second-most aces of the tournament with 36, just behind Naomi Osaka’s 37, and was winning 79 percent of points off her first serve.

That scoreboard pressure figured to be a problem for Gauff, who started Thursday’s semifinal trying to force her way into games on the ground — and a shaky start serving didn’t help.

She started leeching points, hitting a double fault, then a forehand error in the third set to hand Muchová a 2-1 lead to start. A badly missed overhead at 3-1, 30-40 on Gauff’s serve put Muchová up 4-1 in a flash. In the following game, Gauff pushed her opponent to 0-40 before Muchová forced a few backhand errors from Gauff and won five straight points to close Gauff’s window for a comeback another inch. In 39 minutes, she had the first set.

But none of that had much to do with Muchová’s serve. Her percentage of first serves in was in the low 40s, and it never got much higher than 50. Gauff just made errors on the biggest points, break points against her and break points on her opponent’s serve, too.

But as she has so often this tournament, Gauff yanked momentum back in her direction in the second set. The Floridian loosens up the heat, and as the temperatures climbed above 90 degrees Fahrenheit, she chipped away at Muchová’s serve just as she did in the opener.

But this time, when she got herself three break points in the fourth game of the set, she didn’t let a couple of good serves fluster her. She relinquished two break points, took a breath, and on the third chased down Muchová’s short ball to the corner and sent it back at the same angle to take the game — then let out a roar.

Muchová faded from the set after that, leaving the court at the set break while Gauff remained, unbothered by the sun and the sweat glistening on her shoulders. The third essentially went by in a flash, tightening as Muchová made the kind of mistakes she often does against Gauff, going for the wrong choices in promising situations because of her opponent’s defense.

But in the tiebreak, she found her attacking range — and her route into a final that her game always suggested it might deliver.
